# Example-
# And another example-

> At the onset of the monsoon, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew away to <term>Manasa</term> <gloss>a sacred lake in the Himalayas</gloss>. One-eighth of the flock flew up from the water's edge and went to a forest of land-lilies. Oh young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great passion in the water beautified by young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. 3.

**Prose Order:** Oh girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans went to <term>Manasa</term> lake. One-eighth part flew from the shore and reached a forest of land-lilies. Three pairs of swans were seen eagerly engaged in playful sport in water adorned with tender lotus fibers. Then, tell the total count of the entire flock. 3.

**Meaning:** Oh beloved, sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. Among them, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root went to <term>Manasaro-vara</term> lake. One-eighth part of the flock flew from the edge of the water into a forest of land-lilies. Six swans <note>three pairs</note> were seen playing very affectionately in water glowing with tender lotus stalks. Tell me, how many swans were in that group? 3.

**Mathematical Setup:** Multiplier of the square root is 10. The fraction is <gloss>1/8</gloss>. The visible quantity is <gloss>6</gloss>. As the rule states "when increased or decreased by fractions," here we divide the visible quantity and the square root multiplier by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The resulting visible quantity is <gloss>48/7</gloss>. The square root multiplier becomes <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Its square <gloss>1600/49</gloss> added <note>to the product of the visible quantity and the denominator</note> results in <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result gives the total flock of swans: 144.

**Explanation:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one <note>the whole</note>, so <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> = <gloss>7/8</gloss>. This was divided into the visible quantity 6, resulting in <gloss>6/1 / 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. Thus, <gloss>48/7</gloss> became the adjusted visible quantity. Similarly, the square root multiplier 10 was divided by the remaining fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>, so <gloss>10/1 / 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. This became the adjusted multiplier. Now, treating <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the multiplier, the operation was performed according to the method in the previous verse. Specifically, half of the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> was taken. Its square was <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. This was added to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

<summary>This page presents a poetic mathematical problem involving a flock of swans to demonstrate the solution of quadratic equations. It provides the verse, a prose explanation, and a step by step calculation resulting in the number 144.</summary>
<keywords>Lilavati, Bhaskara II, quadratic equations, square roots, fractions, algebra, swans, mathematical poetry</keywords>

Vasudeva is the Supreme Brahman <gloss>the absolute reality</gloss>. His form is the Supreme Spirit <note>original: "Param Purusha"</note>. He is unmanifest, devoid of qualities <gloss>nirguna</gloss>, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five elements, and imperishable, meaning he is free from any change or decay.

->The God within nature, moving everywhere both outside and inside, is Sankarshana; having first created the waters, he cast his seed into them.<-

Since the pure Brahman cannot be the direct cause of the material world, it is said: he is situated within nature <note>original: "prakrityantargato"</note>, conditioned by the creative power <gloss>maya</gloss>, and moves everywhere outside and inside because he is the material cause of the universe. All these attributes of Sankarshana, who is an expansion of Vasudeva, should be understood through his identification with the essence of Vasudeva. Sankarshana, as an expansion of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, he cast his seed, which is a specific power <gloss>shakti</gloss>.

The deity Sankarshana, who is experienced everywhere, entered into this nature and first created the waters. Afterward, he established his brilliance in the form of a seed within that water.

->That became a golden egg, surrounded everywhere by darkness; within it, Aniruddha, the eternal, first became manifest.<-

What happened next is explained: That water, combined with that power, became a golden egg <note>original: "haimam"</note> in a spherical shape, covered everywhere—inside and out—by darkness. This means the golden egg was produced in the sky accompanied by darkness. Inside that golden egg, Aniruddha—who is eternal, constant, and an expansion of Sankarshana (himself an expansion of Vasudeva)—became manifest. He was not "born" or "produced" in the sense of coming into existence from nothing, but rather became visible. This follows the doctrine of existent effects <note>original: "Satkaryavada"</note>, which holds that the effect already exists within the cause. Just as oil is already present in sesame seeds and is merely expressed, he was manifested, not created.

That seed-like brilliance took the form of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. There, within the egg, the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared.

->He is recited in the Vedas as the Lord Hiranyagarbha; he is called Aditya because he was the first manifestation, and Surya because of his expansion.<-

Now, his other names are given for the easy understanding of the world. This Aniruddha, an expansion of Sankarshana, is endowed with the six-fold lordly powers <term>shaigunya-aishvarya</term> <gloss>the six divine attributes: sovereignty, virility, glory, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion</gloss>. In the Vedas <note>original: "chhandasi"</note>, he is described as Hiranyagarbha <gloss>the Golden Embryo</gloss> because he resided within the interior of the golden egg. This is his famous alternative name in the Vedas. He is certainly called Aditya because he was the first to be manifested. Because of his expansion or emergence from this world, he is called Surya.

The scripture <note>original: "shruti"</note> states: Hiranyagarbha was present in the beginning; when born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.

This is the Lord Hiranyagarbha who is mentioned in the Vedas. First—

<summary>This page describes the cosmogony of the Surya Siddhanta, detailing the manifestation of the divine expansions Sankarshana and Aniruddha within a golden egg to begin the process of creation. It identifies the creator deity with Vedic figures like Hiranyagarbha and Surya.</summary>
<keywords>Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Aniruddha, Hiranyagarbha, golden egg, cosmogony, Satkaryavada, Aditya, Surya, Prakriti</keywords>

# Chapter 3: Examination of Feelings

A wise man, even if he is confident in his own abilities, should not pursue a woman who is suspicious, closely guarded, fearful, or under the strict watch of her mother-in-law. <note>verse 27</note>

Thus ends the second chapter, titled Strategies for Seducing Women through Familiarity, in the fifth book on Extramarital Affairs <term>Paradarika</term> of the <term>Kamasutra</term> by Shri Vatsyayana.

<margin>Suspicious refers to one who doubts the suitor. Guarded refers to those protected by guards. Fearful refers to fear of the husband. Under a mother-in-law refers to those living under her authority. He should not pursue means he should not desire her, knowing his own limits and realizing that success here is unlikely.</margin>

This concludes the forty-fourth topic: Strategies for Seduction <term>Abhiyoga</term>.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled Strategies for Seducing Women through Familiarity, in the fifth book on Extramarital Affairs of the <term>Jayamangala</term> commentary on the <term>Kamasutra</term> composed by Yashodhara.

## Chapter 3

### The Examination of Feelings <term>Bhavapariksha</term>

Even when seduction is attempted, women who are steady and bold must be tested. Because their true intentions are not easily revealed, one cannot use specialized methods of seduction without first understanding their heart. Therefore, the examination of feelings is now discussed:

A man who is making an approach should observe the behavior of the woman; through her actions, her feelings are tested. <note>verse 1</note>

<margin>Just as one approaches a young maiden, he should observe her tendencies and gestures. By examining these, her internal state is revealed.</margin>

How is she to be won? The author says:

If she does not reveal her secret thoughts, he should win her over through a female messenger. <note>verse 2</note>

<margin>Not revealing her secret means she does not openly show her desire for union. Because she is bold and mature, he should use a messenger to reach her.</margin>

If she rejects the initial approach but continues to associate with him, he should understand that her mind is divided into two. He should win her over gradually. <note>verse 3</note>

<margin>After rejecting the advances made by the hero and staying away for some days, if she then seeks out his company again, he should know she is of two minds. She may be thinking, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over step by step and not abandon her suddenly.</margin>

The author states a specific detail here:

If she rejects the advance but is seen again even more exquisitely adorned, and in that same state she approaches him...

<summary>This page concludes the chapter on techniques of seduction and begins the chapter on testing a woman's true feelings. It emphasizes observing a woman's behavioral cues and using messengers when she is hesitant or of two minds.</summary>
<keywords>Kamasutra, Vatsyayana, Bhavapariksha, examination of feelings, seduction strategies, messenger, Yashodhara, Jayamangala</keywords>

It should be given; and its final outcome is within his control. Therefore, you must take it away. Having heard this, as soon as he woke up, he searched for the bag of gold. Seeing that it was empty, he thought: Oh! How has the money I earned with such great hardship vanished so easily? Now that I am penniless and useless, how will I show my face to my wife or my friends? Having decided this, he went back to the city of Vardhamanapur. There, after working for another year and earning five hundred gold pieces, he set out for his home again by a different route.

Just as the sun was setting, he arrived at that very same banyan tree. Oh, the misery! Oh, the pain! Why has cursed fate started this again? That same demon in the form of a banyan tree has appeared once more. Thinking thus, as if in a dream, he saw those same two men upon a branch of the tree. One of them said: Creator! Why did you give these five hundred gold pieces to this Somilaka? Do you not know that he is not meant to have anything more than food and clothing? The other replied: O Action! I must certainly give to those who are industrious. Its final outcome is within his control. So why do you reproach me? Having heard this, as soon as Somilaka searched for his bag, he saw that it was empty. Then, overcome by supreme despair, he thought: Oh! What is the use of my life without wealth? Therefore, I will abandon my life by hanging myself here from this banyan tree.

Having made this decision, he fashioned a rope out of <term>darbha</term> <gloss>sacred kusha grass</gloss>, placed the noose around his neck, climbed a branch, and just as he was about to tie it and throw himself off, a man standing in the sky spoke these words: O Somilaka! Do not, do not commit such a rash act. I am that same taker of your wealth, who allowed you nothing more than food and clothing.

<summary>The weaver Somilaka loses his hard earned wealth twice due to the intervention of personified forces of Fate and Action. In despair, he attempts to hang himself from a banyan tree but is interrupted by a divine voice.</summary>
<keywords>Somilaka, Weaver, Fate, Action, Vardhamanapur, Banyan tree, gold, suicide, wealth, industry</keywords>

# Hitopadesha

-> 140 <-

Since the time for war <note>original: <term>vigraha</term></note> has arrived, why does the King not prepare for battle beforehand? For it is said: What kind of servant or what kind of minister is he who, without any consideration, directs the King toward military engagement and the abandonment of his own position at the very beginning?

Furthermore: One should strive to conquer enemies by any means other than war. Victory is seen to be uncertain when two sides are fighting.

And another thing: One should strive to overcome the enemy through conciliation <note>original: <term>sama</term></note>, gifts <note>original: <term>dana</term></note>, or sowing dissension <note>original: <term>bheda</term></note>, used either separately or all together; but never through war.

Moreover: Every person is a hero as long as they have not encountered a real conflict. Who is not prideful before they have witnessed the strength of the opponent?

Additionally: A great result is not achieved by creatures through harsh means as effectively as it is through mild efforts. Achievement comes from small means. However, seeing that war is at hand, let it be regarded with caution <note>original: <term>avajñīyatām</term> suggests looking down upon or treating it with strategic disregard</note>. For it is said:

When the battle is imminent, the Chakravaka <gloss>ruddy sheldrake or Brahminy duck, serving here as a wise minister</gloss> says: O Great King, war is not the first duty. What kind of servant or minister is he who advises the King to prepare for battle and leave his own place without prior deliberation? Furthermore, one should try to defeat the enemy through conciliation and other peaceful means; never by battle. This is because between two combatants, it is not known for certain who will be the victor. Furthermore, one should strive to resolve the enemy through conciliation, gifts, or dissension, either individually or collectively; never through war. Furthermore, all people are brave as long as they have not fought.

<summary>The minister Chakravaka advises the King against jumping into immediate warfare, emphasizing that diplomacy and strategic means like conciliation or bribery are preferable to the uncertainty of battle.</summary>
<keywords>Hitopadesha, diplomacy, war strategy, Chakravaka, conciliation, Sanskrit fables, political ethics</keywords>

## Jiaona

Scholar Kong, given the name Xueli, was a descendant of the Sage <note>Confucius</note>. He was a man of refined character and a skilled poet. A close friend of his, serving as an official in Tiantai, sent a letter inviting him to visit. When Kong arrived, the friend had unfortunately died. Kong was left stranded and destitute with no way to return home. He took up residence at Putuo Temple, where he was employed by the monks to transcribe texts.

About a hundred paces west of the temple stood the estate of a Mr. Shan. Mr. Shan was the descendant of a noble family, but because of a major lawsuit, his fortunes had declined and his household had dwindled. He had moved his family to the countryside, leaving the house in town vacant. 

One day, the snow fell in heavy drifts and there were no travelers on the road. As Kong happened to pass by the gate of the estate, a young man came out. His appearance and manner were very elegant. Seeing Kong, he hurried over to greet him with a bow and invited him inside with many kind words of consolation. Kong took a liking to him and followed him in. The rooms were not very large, but every wall was draped with brocade curtains and hung with the calligraphy and paintings of ancient masters. On the desk lay a book with a label that read: "Trifles from Langhuan" <note>Langhuan refers to a mythical library of the immortals</note>.

<summary>Scholar Kong, stranded after the death of a friend, is invited into a mysterious and elegant estate by a refined young man during a snowstorm.</summary>
<keywords>Scholar Kong, Jiaona, Putuo Temple, Mr. Shan, Langhuan, Pu Songling, ghost story, refined scholar</keywords>

Together, they provided farmland and a residence for Cheng. This angered the elder brothers, who viewed it as a hollow display of generosity. They went to Cheng's home to harass and insult him. Having spent a long time among bandits, Cheng was accustomed to forceful and fierce behavior. Hearing their insults, he grew furious and said, "Now that I have returned, no one was willing to provide me with a roof over my head. Fortunately, my third brother cared for our sibling bond, yet you now punish him for it? Do you intend to drive me away?" 

He threw a stone at Xiao <note>The eldest brother</note>. Ren and Yi <note>The second and third brothers</note> both came out with staffs. Cheng seized Zhong and Xin <note>The sons of the elder brothers</note> and beat them both countless times. Before they could bring a lawsuit against him, Cheng sued them first. The magistrate sent someone to consult Youyu <note>The youngest brother</note>. Youyu had no choice but to go. He stated that he was deeply ashamed of himself and remained silent, only weeping. When pressed for an answer, he only begged the official to deliver a just verdict. The magistrate then ruled that Xiao and the others must each give up a portion of their farmland and property to Cheng, so that the estate was divided into seven equal parts. 

From this point on, Ren and Yi showed Cheng even greater love and respect than before. During a conversation, they suddenly spoke of their mother's burial, and all three wept. Cheng said with determination, "To be so unkind as to leave her thus is to be no better than a beast." He then wished to open the grave and rebury her. Ren and Yi ran to tell Youyu. Youyu hurried home to advise against it, but Cheng would not listen and set a date for the task.

<summary>Cheng violently defends himself against his elder brothers' harassment and wins a legal settlement for his share of the family estate. He later insists on reburying his mother despite Youyu's objections.</summary>
<keywords>Liaozhai Zhiyi, Pu Songling, family dispute, inheritance, filial piety, legal judgment, reburial</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: describing a violent altercation where someone was beaten with boards and sticks while standing, leaving two gashes on their face.</meta>

"They used boards and sticks on him while he was standing there. I do not know what implement was used, but he was beaten severely, and his face was cut in two places. We heard that your mother has a certain type of medicine here for treating staff wounds <note>The 'staff' or 'board' was the standard instrument for corporal punishment in a domestic or legal setting.</note>. Would you look for a pill to give me, Miss?"

When Bao-chai heard this, she quickly ordered Ying-er to find two pills and give them to Ping-er. Bao-chai said, "Since this is the case, please convey my regards to her on my behalf. I shall not go myself." Ping-er gave her word to Bao-chai and departed. This matter requires no further comment.

We turn now to Xiang-ling. After meeting the others and finishing her evening meal, she saw Bao-chai and the rest leave for her mother’s quarters. Xiang-ling then made her way to the瀟湘館 <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>The Bamboo Lodge, residence of Lin Dai-yu</gloss>. By this time, Dai-yu was mostly recovered from her illness. Seeing Xiang-ling come into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiang-ling said with a smile, "Now that I have moved in and have some free time, if you would only teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!"

Dai-yu smiled and replied, "Since you want to learn to compose poetry, you must acknowledge me as your master. Although I am not an expert, I know enough to teach you the basics." Xiang-ling laughed, "If that is truly the case, I shall take you as my master. You must not grow weary of me."

Dai-yu said, "What difficulty is there in this that makes it worth such fuss? It is nothing more than the four stages: the opening, the development, the transition, and the conclusion <note>original: "qi cheng zhuan he," the structural requirement for regulated verse</note>. Within the development and transition sections, there are two pairs of couplets. Tonal level sounds must be matched against deflected sounds; empty words against solid words, and solid words against empty words <note>This refers to the grammatical and tonal parallelism required in Chinese poetry, where 'solid' words are nouns and 'empty' words are particles or abstract terms</note>. If you truly have a brilliant line, you may even disregard these rules of tone and structure."

Xiang-ling laughed, "No wonder when I occasionally steal a look at one or two poems in old books, some couplets are perfectly matched while others are not. I also heard people say, 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be precise.' Yet in the poems of the ancients, some follow this and some are wrong in the even-numbered positions. I have been confused every day. Now that I hear you speak, it seems these rules are not so rigid after all, as long as the phrasing is fresh and original."

Dai-yu said, "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is ultimately a secondary matter; the most important thing is the conception. If the intent and flavor are authentic, the poem will be good even without polished phrasing. This is what is called 'not letting the words damage the meaning.'"

Xiang-ling said, "I simply love Lu Fang-weng's <note>Lu You, a famous Southern Song dynasty poet</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Dai-yu replied, "It is because you do not yet understand poetry that you love such shallow and accessible things. Once you fall into that pattern, you will never be able to break out of it to learn better things. Listen to me: if you truly wish to learn, I have here the *Collected Works of Wang Mo-jie* <note>Wang Wei, a Tang dynasty master known for his Buddhist-influenced nature poetry</note>. Take his hundred five-character regulated verses and study them until you have thoroughly mastered them. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu, the 'Poet-Historian' of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character regulated verses. After that, read one or two hundred of Li Qing-lian's <note>Li Bai, the 'Poet-Immortal' of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three men as your foundation, you can look at Tao Yuan-ming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and the others. With a person as clever and bright as you are, in less than a year, you need not worry about becoming a true poet!"

Hearing this, Xiang-ling smiled, "In that case, dear Miss, please bring the book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems tonight." At these words, Dai-yu ordered Zi-juan to bring Wang the Right Vice-President’s <note>An official title for Wang Wei</note> five-character regulated verses. Handing them to Xiang-ling, she said, "Only read the ones marked with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress Bao-chai, or if you see me, I will explain it to you."

Xiang-ling took the poems and returned to the 蘅蕪院 <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>The All-Spice Court, residence of Xue Bao-chai</gloss>. Ignoring all other affairs, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Bao-chai urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her so devoted, Bao-chai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just as Dai-yu had finished her morning washing and grooming, Xiang-ling arrived with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Dai-yu smiled and asked, "How many do you remember?" Xiang-ling laughed, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." Dai-yu asked, "Have you gained any insights?" Xiang-ling smiled, "I have gained some understanding, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you what I think."

<summary>Xiang-ling moves into the Grand Prospect Garden and asks Lin Dai-yu to teach her how to compose poetry. Dai-yu provides a curriculum focused on Tang dynasty masters and emphasizes that poetic meaning is more important than rigid formal rules.</summary>
<keywords>Xiang-ling, Lin Dai-yu, poetry, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, literary education, Grand Prospect Garden, regulated verse</keywords>

Previously, Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to promote famous scholars to gain public prestige. Most officials followed this path, and thus he recommended the talent of Cai Yong. Zhuo ordered his summons, but Yong initially did not intend to go. Zhuo, enraged, sent a messenger to tell Yong: "If you do not come, I will exterminate your entire clan." Yong was terrified and had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Zhuo was greatly pleased to see Yong and promoted his rank three times within a single month, appointing him as <term>Shizhong</term> <gloss>Palace Attendant</gloss>. He was treated with great intimacy and favor. <gloss>Just as Yang Xiong relied on Wang Feng, Yong was fated to be consumed like firewood from Mount Kunshan.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Former Emperor <note>Shao Di, Liu Bian</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were imprisoned in the Everlasting Peace Palace. Their clothing and food supplies gradually dwindled. The Former Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>This mirrors what a later king said: "The days and months in this place are unbearable."</gloss> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and composed a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds soar and dance; in the cold, abandoned palace, he is solitary and aged before his time.</gloss> The poem read:

The tender grass is green, condensed in mist,
The pair of swallows fly, fluttering and twisting.
The Luo River flows, a single vein of blue,
People on the path are envied by all. <gloss>The first half of the poem describes the swallows and the view from afar.</gloss>

Deep within the emerald clouds is the hall where I once lived. <gloss>His eyes are fixed on his former palace, but he cannot fly there; he is truly inferior to the swallows who can return to their old nests. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will uphold loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the resentment within my heart? <gloss>The second half is his personal lament. The poetry is fine.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo frequently sent people to spy on them. On this day, they obtained this poem and presented it to him. Zhuo said, "Complaining and writing poetry gives me a justification to kill him." <gloss>To kill him with a stated reason is also a way to instruct the world.</gloss> He then ordered Li Ru to take eighteen warriors into the palace to assassinate the Emperor. The Emperor, the Empress Dowager, and the Consort were upstairs when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was greatly alarmed. Ru offered the Emperor <term>zhenjiu</term> <gloss>poisoned wine</gloss>. <gloss>Since the poem mentioned wine, this drink is a most elegant response.</gloss>

<summary>Dong Zhuo forces the scholar Cai Yong into service and discovers a poem written by the deposed Emperor Shao Di expressing grief. Using the poem as a pretext for treason, Zhuo sends Li Ru to the palace to execute the imperial family with poisoned wine.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhuo, Li Ru, Cai Yong, Shao Di, Empress Dowager He, Consort Tang, assassination, poisoned wine, poetry, Romance of the Three Kingdoms</keywords>

# Sutrasthana Chapter 19 (143)

In this manner, having removed the waste material, the expert physician should seat the patient. For wounds caused by <term>kapha</term> <gloss>phlegm or water humor</gloss> and <term>vayu</term> <gloss>wind humor</gloss>, the waste should be squeezed and removed several times. <note>verse 39</note> Pressing the wound from the bottom, the physician should drain the discharge according to the direction of hair growth. All hidden joints and connections must be properly aligned. <note>verse 40</note> In joining the lips, one should follow the methods previously described. A physician knowledgeable in joints should also use their intellect to apply the appropriate bandages for broken bones as prescribed. <note>verse 41</note>

Whether rising, sitting, going to bed, walking, or traveling by various vehicles, the wound of such a person <note>who is properly bandaged</note> does not suffer harm. <note>verse 42</note> Wounds located in the joints, bones, or internal cavities, as well as those in the veins and tendons, deep-seated wounds, and those that are uneven in all directions, cannot be successfully treated without the proper application of bandages. <note>verse 43</note>

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Sutrasthana of the <term>Sushruta Samhita</term>. <note>chapter 18</note>

Whether rising, sitting, lying down, walking, or riding, the wound of a person <insert>properly bandaged</insert> does not cause pain. <note>Hindi commentary on verse 42</note> Wounds in the joints, bones, and cavities, those in the veins and tendons, thick and deep wounds, and those that have become irregular on all sides cannot be cured without the prescribed bandages. <note>Hindi commentary on verse 43</note>

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Sutrasthana in the Hindi commentary on the <term>Sushruta Samhita</term> by Pandit Muralidhar Sharma. <note>chapter 18</note>

### Chapter Nineteen 19

Now, we shall explain the chapter regarding the nursing and care of the wounded <note>original: Vranitopasaniya</note>.

Here begins the explanation of the chapter named <term>Vranitopasaniya</term> <gloss>the method of behavior and care for the wounded</gloss>.

First, one should seek a room for the wounded patient.
